extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and critics interested in biblical criticism and the arguments of Thomas Paine (readers of Age of Reason)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and argumentative tests used to evaluate the truth, authorship, and authenticity of biblical narratives (especially the New Testament) by examining internal consistency, plausibility, authorship claims, omissions, and literary signs of fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement vs disagreement of parts as test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "The agreement of all the parts of a story does not prove that story to be true, because the parts may agree, and the whole may be false; secondly, that the disagreement of the parts of a story proves the whole cannot be true."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal consistency as a decisive negative test: while mutual agreement among parts is not proof, contradictions among accounts (timing, persons, events) demonstrate falsity. Examples given: contradictory genealogies, differing resurrection appearances and locations among the four Gospels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions among gospel accounts undermine eyewitness credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagreements in detail between Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John (time/place/participants of events) imply the writers were not eyewitnesses and therefore their authority is undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare parallel passages for concrete contradictions: genealogies, hour of crucifixion (Mark: third hour vs John: sixth hour), wording of inscription on cross, darkness/earthquake/graves opening (reported by Matthew but omitted by others), differing accounts of the women at the tomb, number/position of angels, and differing post-resurrection meeting locations (Galilee vs Jerusalem vs Emmaus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genealogical inconsistency as evidence of fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: The genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke contradict each other in nearly every particular (different names and counts of generations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete mismatch: Matthew lists 28 generations from David to Christ (27 full generations), Luke lists 43; only David and Joseph agree between lists. Use generation counts and implausible generational intervals (e.g., average 40 years in Matthew) to argue improbability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence/omission by other writers indicates non-occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: If extraordinary or public events (e.g., earthquake, graves opening, army of saints walking into the city) had happened, all writers and contemporaries would have reported them; their omission in other accounts is evidence they did not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an event is of such notoriety that independent authors would have recorded it. Omission is especially suspicious for supernatural occurrences that would strengthen the narrative (resurrection signs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronistic language signals late composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that imply distance in time (e.g., 'this saying ... is commonly reported among the Jews until this day') indicate the narrator was writing long after the event and not a contemporary eyewitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek linguistic markers implying 'until this day' or similar temporal perspective; treat them as evidence the text was composed generations later rather than by contemporaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implausible logistics/incoherent testimony indicates fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative logistics that cannot reasonably occur (e.g., guards asleep who nevertheless identify perpetrators; witnesses giving detailed testimony while asleep) reveal the story's absurdity and fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the described sequence of actions and witness capabilities are coherent. The Matthew guard/watch story is used as an example of logically impossible testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite or patched prayers/texts suggest invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prayer constructed from various Psalms 'without connection or consistency, and adapted to the distress, but not at all to the condition' indicates a made-up composition rather than an authentic utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze stylistic and lexical fit between quoted material and the narrated situation. If the prayer/text is a mosaic of earlier material awkwardly fitted, consider it contrived (example: Jonah's prayer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity or ludicrous elements in faith-stories indicate fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscene or ludicrous elements (e.g., a virgin birth described as a woman 'debauched by a ghost') are tokens of fable and imposture rather than serious revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat narratives that reduce to indecent or mythic parallels (Jupiter and Leda/Europa analogies) as signs the story derives from mythology, not historic fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrofitting/unriddling of prophetic/poetical passages is unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecies are often poetical flights and metaphors that priests later 'unriddle' to fit events; such post hoc interpretation cannot establish genuine prophetic prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate poetical/metaphorical language from predictive specificity. Beware interpretations imposed by later authorities to make verses appear prophetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private/skulking appearances vs public appearances as a credibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency in the accounts to make resurrection appearances private and secretive rather than public undermines their value as proof and suggests fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether reported appearances are public and could be freely confirmed. Private, furtive sightings that vary between accounts are suspicious because they fail to achieve the putative aim of convincing the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on a single non-eyewitness's testimony is weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that many people saw an event, when reported only by a single author (e.g., Paul's claim that 500 saw Christ), do not constitute strong corroboration if those witnesses are not directly recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish first-person multiple-witness testimony from secondhand claims; treat solitary attestations of mass sightings skeptically, especially when the author himself earlier disbelieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural claims demand exceptional corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Supernatural events (resurrections, saints rising from graves) require broad, explicit, contemporaneous corroboration; small or isolated mentions are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require multiple independent, detailed attestations for supernatural claims. The absence of corroboration across the Gospels for major miracles is used as evidence against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivial disagreements accumulate to discredit authorship claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Even small contradictions (who said what, precisely where angels sat, whether women entered the tomb) show the writers were not present and thus cannot be credited as inspired eyewitnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogue minor discrepancies; argue that accumulation of trivial differences reduces overall trust in the narrative and its ascribed authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbable narrative elements (miraculous swallowing, overnight gourds) indicate fable or satire
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story contains highly improbable or fantastical incidents (e.g., a great fish swallowing Jonah whole; a gourd growing overnight and dying next morning), treat them as satirical or fable-like inventions rather than literal history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the incident serves a satirical/moral point; if so, interpret as fable or allegory rather than historical report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship uncertainty (no direct proof) weakens belief
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no direct proof that the books were written by the persons they are ascribed to (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), the state of doubt is the opposite of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand external attestation or contemporaneous authorship claims; absence leaves the reader with doubt and undermines claims of apostolic origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal chronological/math checks for plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple chronological arithmetic (e.g., 1080 years between David and Christ divided by 27 generations implying implausible ages at fatherhood) exposes implausible genealogical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply basic historical/chronological calculations to genealogies and generational claims to test plausibility; large averages (e.g., 40 years per generation) are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative function (satire/moral) can explain invented details
rubrics_metrics.description: Some episodes (Jonah's story, the gourd, prophet's malevolence) operate as satire or moral lesson aimed at criticizing prophets or priestly judgment rather than as factual history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a passage fits a didactic or satirical pattern, prefer interpretive readings (allegory/fable) over literal historicity; examine whether the details primarily serve a rhetorical/moral purpose.
